analysis.one_liner: Bans ultraprocessed foods and specific additives, including several food dyes, from school lunches.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on April 1, 2025, referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and has received no cosponsors and no committee action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National School Lunch Act to require that school lunches in the program exclude ultraprocessed foods, as defined by the NOVA classification system, and foods containing potassium bromate, propylparaben, titanium dioxide, brominated vegetable oil, and several food dyes such as yellow dye 5 and red dye 3 [S2][S3]. The federal program serves meals to tens of millions of schoolchildren nationwide. The bill would tighten minimum nutrition standards that all participating schools must follow [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Children who eat school lunches would get meals free of ultraprocessed foods and a list of specific additives and dyes. Schools would gain clearer federal standards, though they would also bear the burden of changing menus and suppliers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the school lunch program's minimum nutrition rules to prohibit ultraprocessed foods as defined by group 4 of the NOVA classification system

Prohibits foods containing potassium bromate, propylparaben, titanium dioxide, brominated vegetable oil, and specific food dyes including yellow dye 5, yellow dye 6, blue dye 1, blue dye 2, green dye 3, red dye 3, and red dye 40

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and suppliers that would have to reformulate or withdraw products from the school lunch market, and school districts that would have to source compliant foods and adjust menus, with possible cost effects passed to school meal budgets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Processed food makers and school meal suppliers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans all group-4 NOVA 'ultraprocessed' foods [S3], a broad category that can include everyday products like whole-grain breads, fortified cereals, and flavored yogurts, so schools could struggle to build menus that still meet other federal nutrition and calorie requirements without them

A nationwide ban on these ingredients would force food suppliers to reformulate or drop school-meal products, and any higher sourcing costs would land on school meal budgets, which already run on thin margins

Health effects of many of these additives at typical exposure levels are still debated, and a single federal standard removes flexibility that some school nutrition professionals argue is better handled case by case

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Removing banned additives and ultraprocessed foods from school meals would likely benefit children's health, and several of the listed additives are already banned or restricted elsewhere. The main cost is practical: the NOVA definition of ultraprocessed is broad and hard to apply at scale, so schools may face menu and sourcing challenges before the benefits arrive. A narrower phase-in with school support would have addressed those concerns more directly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and has seen no further action, no cosponsors, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kennedy introduced the bill in the House on April 1, 2025
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day
No hearings, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled; the only recorded actions are introduction and committee referral

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, processed food suppliers to the school lunch program are unaffected, since the bill has not moved. Children's school meals remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food suppliers, for now — bill is stalled

for.name: Mike Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract any cosponsors; it has been awaiting committee action since April 2025.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: There are no votes or competing positions to judge; a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors is the entire record [S4].

industries.note: A ban on ultraprocessed foods and listed additives in school lunches would force reformulation or removal of products from a major institutional market. The industry's interest in the bill runs against the children who eat the meals.

industries.industry: School food service suppliers and distributors
industries.note: They would bear costs of sourcing compliant foods and reshaping menus, but could also gain business if contracts shift to suppliers that offer cleaner formulations. Their position depends on how quickly they can adapt.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action after referral in April 2025, the bill faces the typical fate of most single-sponsor bills: it is very unlikely to reach a floor vote this Congress unless the committee decides to act or the additive-ban issue gains broader momentum.
